metadata.note: Morgantown, West Virginia's electric street railway, drawn 1908-1934. Two routes are drawn: downtown to the factories at Sabraton up the Deckers Creek valley (with Jerome Park, the company's own weekend park, on the way), and downtown north along the river to the Seneca glass works. Contemporary descriptions also put cars south toward Durbannah and a Greenmont turnback at the Arch Street 'island'; those are not drawn separately. Four operators ran the system in succession - Union Utility (1908-1912), West Virginia Traction & Electric (1912-1921), West Virginia Utilities (1921-1927) and Monongahela West Penn Public Service (1927-1934) - so each route appears four times, one feature per owner, each in that owner's color (Rule 4). Streetcars were replaced by buses in 1934 after the Sabraton tin plate mill closed. RULE 5 NOTE: no horsecar predecessor is documented for Morgantown, and none is drawn. GEOMETRY WARNING: both routes are approximations over today's street grid, not traced track - see geometry_quality.

segments.note: Downtown Morgantown out along Deckers Creek through Greenmont and Jerome Park to the tin plate mill and the other factories at Sabraton - the system's busiest line, and the one whose closure ended it. Union Utility Co. is the first operator recorded for Morgantown's streetcars, from 1908. Electric cars were running in the town before that - contemporary accounts describe competing traction companies in the early 1900s - but no source checked here gives the year the first electric car ran, so the line is drawn from the first company date that is sourced. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: Downtown Morgantown out along Deckers Creek through Greenmont and Jerome Park to the tin plate mill and the other factories at Sabraton - the system's busiest line, and the one whose closure ended it. Monongahela West Penn Public Service Corp. acquired the Morgantown system in 1927 and bought new Kuhlman cars for it (Nos. 113-115) the same year. Service ended in 1934, when the Sabraton tin plate mill - the biggest traffic source on the system - closed and buses took over; car 114 went to the Monongahela West Penn system elsewhere in the state. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
